这个游戏的好评率之高与我主观感受差距过大，以至于简单翻了一眼攻略还不敢贸然给出差评。快进看了一遍walkthough，为了确定到底是游戏本身问题还是我电波没对上。

游戏的抽象本质无聊透顶，解密方法是完全没有线索的穷举。主线内容是在wiki上的链接列表里一个一个点开，某些可能的链接里会包含线索，然后开始没有目的的胡乱点击文字图片，直到生成key（或者没有）。最可恶的是某些链接永远打不开，而有些链接则有固定可访问时间段，你很容易在第一次尝试后就放弃从而错过。

暗网的猎奇只不过是无聊玩法的皮肤，而你实际上无法对其中内容进行任何互动。无法买麻买枪买色情服务买奴隶，即使这些就在那。结合上述玩法，这个卖点就变成了鸡肋，你完全可以把他替换成任何内容，比如财政新闻，超市目录，都不影响游戏性质。

单纯解密肯定无聊，时间限制算是稍微增加了点紧迫感。更重要的部分是连环杀人/绑架犯机制，创意不错但是实现很差，跟hacker一样。触发机制比较随机，你能做的反制手段就是关灯堵门重启路由。这本身可以是比较精彩的插曲/彩蛋甚至是坏结局，甚至是玩法的一半一半，但是会玩的一般都选择提前关灯避开，这样就变成了没什么意义的困难。我的评价是不如fears to fathom（这名字还真妙）

Welcome to the Game, developed and published by Reflect Studios, is a psychological horror experience that builds fear not through traditional monsters or cinematic spectacle, but through isolation, digital paranoia, and the unsettling atmosphere of the deep web. Released in 2016, the game quickly carved out a reputation for delivering a tense and unforgiving experience that places the player in front of a computer screen and challenges them to survive both online and offline threats. Its premise is deceptively simple: search the anonymous corners of the internet to uncover hidden fragments of a mysterious URL, all while avoiding being tracked, hacked, or abducted.

The entire game unfolds from the perspective of a lone individual sitting in a dimly lit apartment, navigating a fictional deep web browser known as the A.N.N. (Anonymous Node Network). The objective is to locate eight hidden keys scattered across obscure websites and piece them together to access a so-called “Red Room.” While this narrative hook draws from internet folklore, the real horror emerges from the process of exploration. Browsing pages filled with cryptic messages, distorted images, and hidden codes becomes a nerve-wracking activity when every click could expose your virtual identity or trigger unwanted attention. The game cleverly transforms mundane computer interactions into a high-stakes survival scenario.

Mechanically, the experience blends investigative puzzle-solving with real-time survival elements. Players must decode clues embedded in webpages, solve encryption challenges, and respond quickly to hacking attempts. Certain mini-games require rapid completion to prevent catastrophic consequences, adding a layer of urgency to what might otherwise be a slow-paced search process. Meanwhile, external threats exist beyond the screen. Environmental cues—such as footsteps, distant knocks, or sudden power disruptions—signal danger in the apartment itself. Managing lights, security measures, and situational awareness becomes just as important as deciphering online puzzles. This dual-layer tension, between digital vulnerability and physical threat, creates a uniquely immersive horror dynamic.

Atmosphere is the game’s defining strength. Rather than relying heavily on jump scares, it cultivates a constant undercurrent of dread. The apartment setting is sparse and claustrophobic, reinforcing isolation. Sound design amplifies tension through subtle ambient noise, abrupt alerts, and audio cues that force players to remain vigilant. Silence itself becomes unsettling, as long stretches of quiet browsing are punctuated by sudden interruptions that shatter focus. The stripped-down visual presentation enhances immersion, making the experience feel intimate and personal rather than cinematic.

The pacing, however, can be polarizing. Progression depends on careful browsing and pattern recognition, which means sessions can feel repetitive as players revisit sites searching for missed clues. The unforgiving nature of certain threats can also frustrate, especially when failure results in restarting significant portions of progress. The randomness of encounters and the lack of explicit guidance contribute to unpredictability, but they can also make success feel dependent on memorization and trial-and-error rather than pure deduction. For some players, this harsh design reinforces tension; for others, it may feel overly punishing.

Narratively, the game avoids deep exposition, focusing instead on atmosphere and implication. The concept of the Red Room serves as a distant objective rather than a fully developed storyline. This minimalist approach leaves room for interpretation and enhances the feeling of mystery, but it also limits character development and emotional depth. The horror remains situational and psychological rather than narrative-driven, rooted in the anxiety of being watched or traced rather than in complex storytelling.

Despite its rough edges, the game remains memorable because of how effectively it captures modern digital fears. It taps into contemporary anxieties surrounding privacy, anonymity, and the darker corners of online culture. By placing players directly in front of a simulated computer interface, it blurs the line between player and protagonist, intensifying immersion. Few horror titles manage to make typing on a keyboard or clicking through webpages feel genuinely threatening.

Ultimately, it stands as a distinctive entry in indie horror, defined by its commitment to psychological tension and environmental immersion. It may not appeal to those seeking fast-paced action or narrative complexity, but for players who appreciate slow-burn suspense and high-stakes puzzle-solving, it delivers a uniquely unsettling experience. I would like to point out that this studio's games... well, you really can't find anything like it anywhere else. They're deeply immersive, and use realism to heighten the horror tenfold. You can try all you like not to pay attention to the content of the pages you're visiting - but the game's core mechanic of searching for keys that are (sometimes literally) between the lines makes you read and see some truly god awful things. All while you've got two killers after you. Honestly, I'd call this game a sort of pseudo rogue-like. You don't gain anything in the game from dying, but YOU gain knowledge that will help you in the next.

And if that trial-and-error gameplay is not your vibe, you *can* just look everything up. (I would still recommend doing at least a handful of runs blind, however.) It does make the game a lot easier, but not too easy. You still have to pay attention. I actually went into this game knowing quite a few things already from videos I'd watched and things I'd read, and still died several times. I found a lot of joy in covering my blind spots and finally executing a successful run. And it's only five dollars! At the very least, you could treat this game like a demo run for the much more intense sequel.

(And as of writing this review, there's a third game coming soon-ish! so now's as good a time as any to get into it.)

Welcome to the Game, um jogo que eu botava muita fé que ele era divertido e bom, por conta dos vídeos antigos que assistia quando moleque desse jogo. Mas a verdade é que ele é um jogo com uma IA totalmente merda e estranha; e sistema de jogo puzzle minimamente desinteressante!

A princípio da minha análise ser negativa, eu acho que vale a pena você jogar o jogo para ter sua própria experiência. Afinal, cada um tem sua própria opinião. Em meu caso específico, apenas me frustrei por talvez ter colocado muita fé que esse jogo era muito bom, mas não, ele é só medíocre mesmo.

"Ah, mas você nem chegou a terminar o jogo pra ter certeza se é isso mesmo que tu acha!"
Mas eu não preciso terminar um jogo pra dar minha opinião e já ter uma base do que acho sobre o jogo. Particularmente, achei chato, mas repeito e entendendo aqueles que gostam desse jogo. Joguei por uma quantidade de tempo bacana, e pra mim já foi o suficiente! 

Nota final: 6/10
